tips.title: Never lost, never used up
tips.body: Both phrases suggest the energy has gone. Write **dissipated to the surroundings and stored in less useful ways** — it says where the energy went, which is what the mark is for.

tips.title: Less useful means spread out
tips.body: Dissipated energy has not become a worse **kind** of energy — it has been **spread out**. 100 J in a motor turns a wheel; the same 100 J through a room's air does nothing. Usefulness is about **concentration**.

tips.title: Conservation is a free check
tips.body: Add the energy before, add it after. If the totals do not match, the answer is wrong — and you can see that **without knowing the right answer**.

tips.title: Name the cure and what it reduces
tips.body: *Lubrication* is half an answer. *Lubrication reduces friction between the moving parts, so less energy is dissipated as thermal energy* is the whole one.

tips.title: Closed depends on the boundary
tips.body: Around a falling ball alone, energy leaves through air resistance — not closed. Around the ball **and the air**, nothing leaves — closed. The question usually tells you which.

why.matters:
Energy is never destroyed, and yet everything runs down: the ball stops bouncing, the tea goes cold, the phone needs charging. Both are true, and this topic is what reconciles them. The energy is all still there. It has **spread out** into the surroundings, warming them by an amount too small to notice, and spread-out energy cannot be gathered back to do a job.

That is the idea the rest of the course leans on. What matters about energy is not how much there is but how **concentrated** it is, and every real machine lets some of it go.

examples.title: The ball that never comes back to your hand
examples.body:
Drop a ball from 100 cm and it comes back to about 60. Its energy was all in the gravitational store at the top, all in the kinetic store at the floor, and then some of it went missing: the ball squashed and did not spring back perfectly, which warmed it, and you heard the rest leave as the thud.

Each bounce keeps the same fraction, so the heights run 60, 36, 22 cm and by the fifth bounce it is under 8 cm. After three bounces 78% of the energy is in the floor, the ball and the air of the room, and none of it is coming back.

props.caption: The missing height is warmth in the ball and the floor, and the sound of the bounce.

visual.alt: Three bars drawn to scale, a ball dropped from one hundred centimetres bouncing back to sixty and then to thirty six, the shrinking bar being the energy that has spread into the surroundings

examples.title: What the vacuum in a flask is for
examples.body:
A hot drink dissipates its energy by every route it can find: conduction through whatever it touches, convection in the air moving past it, and radiation from its warm surface. Tea in a mug is cold in half an hour because all three are open.

A vacuum flask is a list of answers. Two walls with nothing between them, so there is nothing to conduct through and no air to circulate. Silvered surfaces, so the radiation is reflected back in. A stopper of plastic or cork over the one route left. None of the energy is being made to stay; it is just being given no way out.

examples.title: Where a full battery goes
examples.body:
A phone battery holds about 53 000 J. By the time it is flat, where is that energy? Not gone: every joule of it is in the room.

The screen's light landed on the walls and your face and warmed them. The speaker's sound was soaked up by the curtains and the sofa. The chip turned its share into warmth straight away, which is why the phone is warm to hold. Even the radio signals were mostly absorbed by the walls and the air. The battery's energy has not been used up. It has been spread through the room so thinly that no thermometer could find it.

steps.title: The three things energy can do
steps.body:
Energy can be **transferred usefully**, **stored**, or **dissipated** — but it **cannot be created or destroyed**.

That last part is the **principle of conservation of energy**, and it is the rule everything else in this topic follows from.

**The word to be careful with is *wasted*.** When we say energy is wasted, we do not mean it has gone. It has been **dissipated** — transferred to the surroundings and **stored in less useful ways**, usually as thermal energy spread through the air and the materials around. The energy still exists. It is just spread out too thinly to be useful.

$$\textbf{energy in} = \textbf{useful energy out} + \textbf{energy dissipated}$$

**Four ways to say it, and only one is right for the exam:**

- *the energy is lost* — avoid; it sounds as though it has gone
- *the energy is used up* — wrong; energy is never used up
- *the energy is wasted* — acceptable, and the spec's own word, in quotation marks
- *the energy is dissipated to the surroundings, stored in less useful ways* — **best**

Use the last one. It says where the energy went and why it is no longer useful, which is what the mark is for.

steps.title: Closed systems
steps.body:
A **system** is just the object or group of objects you have decided to think about. A **closed system** is one where **no energy enters or leaves**.

**In a closed system there is no net change to the total energy.** Energy moves between stores inside the system, but the total stays the same.

That gives you a powerful way of checking any answer: **add up the energy before and add it up after. The two must match.**

**An example.** A ball of 200 J of gravitational potential energy falls.

| | Gravitational | Kinetic | Thermal | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 200 J | 0 J | 0 J | **200 J** |
| after | 0 J | 150 J | 50 J | **200 J** |

The gravitational store has emptied. Most of it went into the **kinetic** store; 50 J went into a **thermal** store, warming the ball and the air very slightly through air resistance. Nothing was created and nothing was destroyed — **the total is the same on both lines**.

**Why choosing the system matters.** If you draw the boundary around just the ball, energy leaves it — it is not closed. If you draw the boundary around the ball **and the air around it**, nothing leaves, and it is closed. Whether a system is closed depends on **where you draw the line**, and a question will usually tell you.

steps.title: Where the energy goes
steps.body:
**In all system changes, energy is dissipated, so that it is stored in less useful ways.** Every real process wastes some energy. There is no exception.

**The usual culprits:**

- **Friction** between surfaces that rub. The surfaces warm up, and the thermal energy spreads into the surroundings.
- **Air resistance**, which is friction with the air.
- **Sound**, which carries energy away from a machine and spreads out.
- **Electrical resistance**, which heats a wire whenever a current flows through it.

**Almost all of it ends up as thermal energy in the surroundings.** That is what makes it less useful: it is not that the energy has become a different, worse kind, but that it has been **spread out**. A hundred joules concentrated in a motor can turn a wheel. The same hundred joules spread through the air of a room, raising its temperature by a thousandth of a degree, can do nothing.

**Reducing the dissipation.** Because the causes are known, so are the cures:

- **Lubrication** — oil between rubbing surfaces reduces friction.
- **Streamlining** — a smoother shape reduces air resistance.
- **Thermal insulation** — reduces the rate of energy transfer out of a building.
- **Thicker wires** — lower resistance, so less heating for the same current.

Each of these is worth a mark, and each is worth stating with **what it reduces**: *lubrication reduces friction between the moving parts, so less energy is dissipated as thermal energy*.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. State the principle of conservation of energy.
2. What does it mean to say energy has been dissipated?
3. Give two causes of energy dissipation in a machine with moving parts.

**Part B.**

4. An electric motor is supplied with 500 J and transfers 400 J usefully. How much is dissipated, and where does it go?
5. A kettle takes in 2000 J and transfers 1600 J to the water. How much is wasted?

**Part C.**

6. A student writes: *the energy is lost as heat*. Rewrite this sentence so that it would gain full credit, and explain what was wrong with it.
7. Explain why a closed system's total energy never changes, and give an example of energy moving between stores within one.
8. Explain why dissipated energy is described as being stored in a *less useful* way, rather than as having been destroyed.

For question 6, the problem is with two words, not one.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Nothing is lost, and nothing is used up.** Both phrases suggest the energy has gone, and both will cost you. The energy is **dissipated to the surroundings and stored in less useful ways**. Write that once, properly, and you have the mark that a dozen vaguer sentences would not earn.

**Why *less useful* is the exact right phrase.** The energy has not changed into a worse kind of energy. It has been **spread out**. A hundred joules in a motor can turn a wheel; the same hundred joules spread through a room's air, raising it by a thousandth of a degree, can do nothing at all — not because it is a different quantity, but because it is no longer **concentrated**. Usefulness is about concentration, not about kind. That idea is what the whole topic is really teaching, and saying it is the clearest sign of a top answer.

**Conservation is a checking tool, not just a fact.** Add the energy before, add it after. If they do not match, the answer is wrong — and you can see it is wrong without knowing the right answer. Very few checks in physics are that cheap.

**Whether a system is closed depends where you draw the boundary.** Around a falling ball alone, energy leaves through air resistance and it is not closed. Around the ball **and the surrounding air**, nothing leaves and it is. A question that says *closed system* is telling you the total is fixed; a question that does not is often asking you to notice that it is not.

**Name the cure and what it reduces.** *Lubrication* alone is half an answer. *Lubrication reduces friction between the moving parts, so less energy is dissipated as thermal energy* is the whole one. The same for streamlining and air resistance, insulation and the rate of transfer out of a building.

**Dissipation is not a fault in a design.** Every real process dissipates energy — the spec says *in all system changes*. So a question asking why a machine is not 100% efficient is never answered by *because it is badly made*. It is answered by naming the specific process — friction, resistance, sound — that dissipates energy in **that** machine.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Energy can be **transferred usefully**, **stored**, or **dissipated**.
- Energy **cannot be created or destroyed** — the principle of **conservation of energy**.
- **energy in = useful energy out + energy dissipated**
- In a **closed system** there is **no net change** to the total energy.
- Whether a system is closed depends on **where the boundary is drawn**.
- **In all system changes, some energy is dissipated.** There is no exception.
- Dissipated energy is **transferred to the surroundings and stored in less useful ways**, nearly always as **thermal** energy.
- It is *less useful* because it has been **spread out**, not because it has become a worse kind of energy.
- Causes: **friction**, **air resistance**, **sound**, **electrical resistance**.
- Cures: **lubrication**, **streamlining**, **thermal insulation**, **thicker wires**.
- Name the cure **and what it reduces**.
- Avoid *lost* and *used up*. Say **dissipated**.
- Use conservation as a **check**: the energy before and after must add to the same total.

questions.prompt: A filament lamp is supplied with 100 J of electrical energy and transfers 25 J usefully as light. An LED lamp supplied with the same energy transfers 95 J usefully. Compare the two lamps, explaining what happens to the energy in each.
questions.solution: Both lamps obey the principle of conservation of energy, which states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, so in each case the energy supplied must equal the useful energy transferred plus the energy dissipated. The filament lamp is supplied with one hundred joules and transfers twenty five joules usefully as light, so seventy five joules is dissipated. The LED lamp is supplied with the same one hundred joules and transfers ninety five joules usefully, so only five joules is dissipated. In both cases the dissipated energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings: the filament or the components become hot and warm the air around them. It is important to be clear that this energy has not been destroyed and has not been used up. It has been dissipated, meaning it has been transferred to the surroundings and is now stored in a less useful way. The reason it is less useful is not that it has become a worse kind of energy but that it has been spread out rather than concentrated. Seventy five joules spread through the air of a room raises the temperature by an imperceptible amount and can do no useful job, whereas the same energy concentrated could light a room. The LED therefore dissipates fifteen times less energy than the filament lamp for the same input, which is why filament lamps have largely been replaced, and both lamps obey conservation exactly. The difference between them lies not in the rule but in the proportion of the input that is dissipated.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Conservation applies to both:** energy in = useful out + dissipated.

- **Filament lamp**: $100 - 25 = 75$ J dissipated.
- **LED lamp**: $100 - 95 = 5$ J dissipated.

So the LED dissipates **fifteen times less** for the same input, which is why filament lamps have been replaced.

**Where it goes.** To the **thermal store of the surroundings** — the filament gets hot and warms the air.

**The marks most often missed:**

- The energy is **not destroyed and not used up**. It is **dissipated** — transferred to the surroundings and **stored in less useful ways**.
- It is less useful because it has been **spread out**, not because it has become a worse kind of energy. 75 J through a room's air raises the temperature imperceptibly and can do nothing; concentrated, it could light a room.

**And the point that earns the top band:** both lamps obey conservation **exactly**. The difference is not in the rule but in the **proportion** of the input dissipated.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a closed system, and explain why the total energy in one never changes. Use an example.
questions.solution: A system is simply the object or group of objects that has been chosen for consideration, and a closed system is one in which no energy enters and no energy leaves. Because energy cannot be created or destroyed, and because none is entering or leaving across the boundary, there can be no net change to the total energy of a closed system. Energy can still move freely between the different stores within the system, but every joule that leaves one store must appear in another. A useful example is a ball falling through the air. If the system is taken to be the ball together with the air around it, then no energy crosses the boundary and the system is closed. At the start the ball has two hundred joules in its gravitational potential store and nothing in its kinetic or thermal stores. By the time it lands, the gravitational store has emptied, one hundred and fifty joules has been transferred to the kinetic store, and fifty joules has been dissipated by air resistance into thermal stores in the ball and the surrounding air. The total on both occasions is two hundred joules, so nothing has been created or destroyed and only the distribution between stores has changed. It is worth noting that whether a system counts as closed depends on where the boundary is drawn. If the system had been taken as the ball alone, then the fifty joules transferred to the air would have crossed the boundary and left, so that system would not be closed.

questions.modelAnswer:
**A system** is whatever objects you have chosen to think about. **A closed system** is one in which **no energy enters or leaves**.

**Why the total is fixed.** Energy **cannot be created or destroyed**, and none crosses the boundary — so there can be **no net change to the total**. Energy still moves between stores inside; every joule leaving one store appears in another.

**An example — a falling ball, taking the system as the ball *and the air*:**

| | Gravitational | Kinetic | Thermal | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 200 J | 0 J | 0 J | **200 J** |
| after | 0 J | 150 J | 50 J | **200 J** |

The 50 J was dissipated by **air resistance**. Nothing was created or destroyed; only the **distribution** changed.

**The point that earns the last mark:** whether a system is closed depends on **where the boundary is drawn**. Taking the **ball alone**, that 50 J crosses the boundary and leaves — so that system is **not** closed.

examTechnique.body:
Write that energy is dissipated to the surroundings and stored in less useful ways, rather than lost or used up.

Say where the dissipated energy has gone, not just that it has gone.

Explain less useful as meaning spread out rather than concentrated.

Use conservation as a check: the energy before and after must add to the same total.

When naming a way to reduce dissipation, say what it reduces and what follows from that.

For a question about why a machine is not fully efficient, name the specific process that dissipates energy in that machine.

Read carefully whether a system has been defined as closed, and where its boundary lies.
examinerErrors: Writing that energy is lost, or used up.
Saying dissipated energy has become a lower grade of energy, rather than being spread out.
Naming a cure such as lubrication without saying what it reduces.
Answering why a machine is inefficient with because no machine is perfect.
Forgetting that some energy is dissipated in every real change.
Treating a falling object alone as a closed system when air resistance acts on it.
Failing to state where the dissipated energy has gone.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer never says energy is lost, and can explain why the word matters: the energy is dissipated to the surroundings and stored in less useful ways. It knows that less useful means spread out rather than concentrated, and can say that a hundred joules in a motor and the same hundred through a room's air differ in distribution, not in kind. It uses conservation as a check rather than only as a fact, names the specific process that dissipates energy in the machine in front of it, and notices that whether a system is closed depends entirely on where the boundary has been drawn.
